bull.b: Successful piloted transitions and repeatable public demonstrations provide tangible evidence that the VX4 program is progressing beyond laboratory development. Two aircraft also increase testing capacity, helping generate operational data and reduce technical uncertainty ahead of certification.

The broad partner network can strengthen Vertical’s route to certification, operational integration and eventual commercialization. Collaboration across autonomy, charging, airspace and regulatory validation also supports a more complete platform, potentially improving adoption and execution over time.

Battery replacement tied to each delivered aircraft could create recurring aftermarket revenue in addition to initial aircraft sales. If fleets scale, this installed-base opportunity may improve revenue visibility and customer lifetime economics, while using Vertical’s in-house battery integration capabilities.

bear.b: Vertical has not yet demonstrated commercial revenue scale, while operating losses remain material and core EBIT is negative. This limits internal funding capacity and leaves future earnings dependent on certification, production ramp-up and successful customer conversion rather than established demand.

Negative equity and sizable debt relative to the asset base reduce financial flexibility during the long development cycle. The structure increases recapitalization and dilution risk, and may constrain investment choices if certification or industrialization requires more capital than currently available.

A later certification target postpones the point at which aircraft sales and related services can become meaningful. Combined with substantial projected cash outflows, the delay extends the period of dependence on future financing and government support, increasing execution risk before commercialization.
